candidate_relations.reason: Mesenteric artery aneurysm is the parent vascular lesion and omits inferior mesenteric anatomy plus colonic fistula.
Mesenteric vascular malformation with hemorrhage is related bleeding but conflicts with aneurysm-fistula morphology.
Hematocele names the pelvic/abdominal blood collections, a bleeding manifestation not the IMA aneurysm-fistula.
The label matches the full reference: arteriocolonic fistula of inferior mesenteric artery aneurysm.
Ruptured IMA pseudoaneurysm captures the DSA lesion and hemorrhage but omits the arteriocolonic fistula component.
Visceral artery aneurysm with fistula is the parent composite and lacks IMA and colonic specificity.
Inferior mesenteric artery dissection with hemorrhage asserts a conflicting mechanism versus aneurysm with fistula.
Mesenteric vasculitis is a different inflammatory etiology from IMA aneurysm with colonic fistula.
Vascular disease is a nonspecific parent and omits the IMA aneurysm-fistula object.
Hemorrhagic shock would be a physiologic consequence of bleeding, not the anatomic fistula diagnosis.
Inferior mesenteric artery pseudoaneurysm is the imaged lesion but omits arteriocolonic fistula.
Ruptured pseudoaneurysm is a parent of the bleeding lesion and lacks IMA and fistula specificity.
Spontaneous mesenteric hemorrhage describes bleeding without the required IMA aneurysm-colonic fistula.
IMA aneurysm-colonic fistula is a wording variant of the full reference object.
Mesenteric artery dissection conflicts with aneurysm and omits the colonic fistula.
Bleeding colonic diverticulum is a different lower-GI bleeding source.
Intra-abdominal hemorrhage is the CT bleeding finding, not the IMA aneurysm-fistula diagnosis.
Ruptured superior mesenteric artery aneurysm conflicts on SMA versus IMA anatomy.
Spontaneous splenic artery rupture conflicts on vessel anatomy versus the inferior mesenteric artery.
Trauma is a different etiology and is not described in this presentation.
